chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Qasim ibn al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) who said:
'Whenever you see the scholar in love with his worldly life, then suspect him regarding your religion, for every lover of a thing guards what he loves.'

And he (blessings of Allah be upon him) said: 'Allah revealed to Dawud (peace be upon him): "Do not place between Me and yourself a scholar who is infatuated with the world, lest he block you from the path of My love — for they are bandits on the road to My servants who are devoted seekers. The least of what I shall do to them is that I will remove the sweetness of My intimate discourse from their hearts."'

key_terms.حَلَاوَةَ مُنَاجَاتِي: sweetness of My intimate discourse — the spiritual reward of closeness with Allah in supplication
key_terms.قُطَّاعُ طَرِيقِ: bandits of the road — those who actively obstruct seekers from reaching God
key_terms.مَفْتُوناً بِالدُّنْيَا: infatuated/tempted by the world — one seduced by material concerns
key_terms.مُحِبّاً لِدُنْيَاهُ: love for the worldly life — the defining marker of a compromised scholar

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Sadiq say about following a scholar who loves the world?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) warns that a scholar's love for worldly affairs is grounds for suspecting his religious guidance, since a person inevitably prioritizes what they love. This is reinforced by a divine revelation to Prophet Dawud where Allah warns against allowing worldly-infatuated scholars to mediate one's relationship with God, describing them as spiritual highway robbers who divert sincere seekers from divine closeness. The Imam delivered this teaching to followers who would have recognized the danger of blindly following religious authorities whose worldly ambitions compromise their spiritual integrity.
